title: Thinking About the Consequences in the Moment of Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay makes a counterintuitive argument about decision-making: while weighing consequences is essential, doing so at the actual moment of decision can paralyze a leader and bias their thinking. It draws a parallel to sports psychology, citing neurologist Sian Leah Beilock's experiment with competitive golfers who lost putting accuracy when asked to focus on the mechanics and consequences of their stroke mid-execution. The essay's practical recommendation is to front-load consequence-thinking well before the decision point, then deliberately stay present and consequence-free in the actual moment of choice, treating that discipline as a firewall against decision bias.
points: Thinking through consequences is essential decision-making work, but doing it at the actual moment of choice can paralyze a leader.
Psychologists call this fixation 'maladaptive control' -- it interferes with adapting to the moment at hand.
Neurologist Sian Leah Beilock's golf experiment found that asking golfers to focus on the mechanics and consequences of their putt mid-stroke sharply reduced accuracy.
The recommendation for decision-makers mirrors sports psychology advice to athletes: avoid thinking about mechanics or outcomes during execution.
Good leaders weigh consequences well before the decision point, then deliberately stay in the present at the moment of choice.
quotes: Thinking through the possible consequences and implications of a decision is something all good decision-makers do.
Focusing on the consequences of a decision at the moment of making it can confound the reality we perceive and lead a decision-maker astray.
Psychologists call this maladaptive control, which is a fancy name for actions that prevent people from adapting to the moment at hand.
Thinking about the consequences, the golfers clenched up and lost their fluidity. Not surprisingly, their putting accuracy plummeted.
Thinking in the present is the best firewall against any bias created by the consequences.
